title: Airway, Respiration & Ventilation
summary: How air gets in, how oxygen gets to cells, and every tool an EMT uses when that breaks: positioning, suction, adjuncts, oxygen devices, the bag-valve mask, CPAP and choking. Real numbers for every device, rate and time limit.

lessons.title: Ventilation, oxygenation, respiration
lessons.body:
## Three words that are not the same thing

Most people say breathing for everything the lungs do. The exam splits it into three steps, and each one can fail on its own.

**Ventilation** is air physically moving in and out. It is a mechanical job: the diaphragm drops, the chest gets bigger, pressure inside falls, air rushes in. Someone in a smoke-filled room ventilates perfectly and still dies.

**Oxygenation** is oxygen crossing from the alveoli (the air sacs) into the blood and loading onto hemoglobin in the red cells. A patient in pulmonary edema moves plenty of air and still cannot get oxygen across the fluid.

**Respiration** is the actual gas exchange at the cell: oxygen out of the blood into tissue, carbon dioxide back the other way. Cyanide poisoning wrecks this step while ventilation and oxygenation look perfect.

> **Key:** Oxygen fixes an oxygenation problem. Only positive pressure from a bag-valve mask fixes a ventilation problem. If the patient is not moving enough air, a nonrebreather is the wrong tool.

## Minute volume is the number that matters

Tidal volume is the air in one breath, about `500 mL` in an average adult, roughly `5-7 mL/kg`. Minute volume is tidal volume times respiratory rate.

Not all of it counts. About `150 mL` of every adult breath never reaches an alveolus. It sits in the mouth, trachea and bronchi doing nothing. That is dead space, and it costs the same `150 mL` on every breath no matter how small the breath is.

Compare two adults, both with a minute volume of `6,000 mL`:

| Patient | Tidal volume | Rate | Dead space wasted | Reaching alveoli |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 500 mL | 12 | 1,800 mL | 4,200 mL |
| B | 200 mL | 30 | 4,500 mL | 1,500 mL |

Patient B looks like he is working hard. He is ventilating at roughly a third of patient A. Fast and shallow is a failing patient, and the respiratory rate alone hides it.

## The hypoxic drive myth

Normally, rising carbon dioxide is what makes you breathe. The old teaching says a chronic `COPD` patient who lives with high CO2 loses that drive and breathes only because of low oxygen, so giving oxygen shuts breathing off.

The real mechanism is mostly two other things. High oxygen changes which parts of a damaged lung get blood flow (V/Q mismatch), and it makes hemoglobin release CO2 (the Haldane effect). CO2 can rise. But it rises over many minutes and it is manageable. Hypoxia kills in minutes and it is not.

> **Trap:** Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic COPD patient. Give it, titrate to an `SpO2` of `88-92%` instead of `94-99%`, and keep a bag-valve mask within arm's reach in case the patient gets sleepy and stops ventilating.
keyPoints: Ventilation is air moving, oxygenation is oxygen loading onto blood, respiration is gas exchange at the cell.
Minute volume = tidal volume x rate; fast and shallow moves far less useful air than slow and full.
About 150 mL of every adult breath is dead space and is wasted on every single breath.
Hypoxia kills faster than CO2 retention, so never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic COPD patient.
Target SpO2 94-99% for most patients and 88-92% for known COPD.

checks.q: An adult is breathing 30 times a minute with a tidal volume of about 200 mL. Compared with an adult breathing 12 times a minute at 500 mL, this patient is:
choices: Ventilating better, because the minute volume is higher
Ventilating about the same, because both minute volumes equal 6,000 mL
Ventilating far worse, because dead space eats most of each small breath
Impossible to judge without an arterial blood gas
checks.why: Both have a 6,000 mL minute volume, but the fixed 150 mL of dead space is wasted on every breath. At 30 breaths that is 4,500 mL wasted, leaving only 1,500 mL reaching alveoli versus 4,200 mL for the slower, deeper patient.

checks.q: A COPD patient has an SpO2 of 82% and is visibly struggling. The correct action is:
choices: Apply high-flow oxygen and titrate down toward an SpO2 of 88-92%
Withhold oxygen to protect the hypoxic drive
Give oxygen only by nasal cannula at 2 L/min regardless of response
Wait for capnography before giving any oxygen
checks.why: Hypoxia is the immediate threat. Give oxygen and titrate to 88-92%. Withholding or capping oxygen arbitrarily kills; the CO2 rise from oxygen is slower and manageable, and you keep a bag-valve mask ready in case ventilation fails.

checks.q: Cyanide poisoning impairs which step?
choices: Ventilation
Oxygenation
Both ventilation and oxygenation
Respiration, the gas exchange at the cell
checks.why: Cyanide blocks the cell's ability to use oxygen. Air still moves in and out and hemoglobin still loads oxygen, so ventilation and oxygenation look normal while the cells suffocate.

lessons.title: The airway top to bottom, and why kids are different
lessons.body:
## Upper airway: everything above the vocal cords

Air enters through the nose or the mouth. The nose warms, filters and humidifies it. The mouth is the backup and moves more air faster.

Behind both is the pharynx (throat), split into three floors: the nasopharynx behind the nose, the oropharynx behind the mouth, and the laryngopharynx where the tube divides into two.

At that division sits the epiglottis, a flap of cartilage that folds over the larynx (voice box) every time you swallow, so food goes down the esophagus. In an unresponsive patient that protection is gone.

The larynx holds the vocal cords. In an adult the gap between the cords is the narrowest point of the whole airway. Just below them, the cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage anywhere in the airway.

> **On shift:** The most common airway obstruction in an unresponsive patient is the tongue. The tongue is attached to the jaw, so lifting the jaw lifts the tongue off the back of the throat. That is the entire logic behind head-tilt chin-lift and jaw thrust.

## Lower airway: cords down to the air sacs

Below the cords is the trachea (windpipe), roughly `10-12 cm` long in an adult and held open by C-shaped cartilage rings. It divides at the carina into the right and left mainstem bronchi.

The right mainstem leaves at a straighter angle, which is why aspirated objects, vomit and over-inserted breathing tubes all tend to end up in the right lung.

The bronchi branch into bronchioles, which are small, muscular and have no cartilage. They are what clamps shut in asthma. At the end sit roughly 300 million alveoli, each one cell thick and wrapped in capillaries. A slippery film called surfactant keeps them from collapsing.

Breathing is muscle work. The diaphragm drops, the intercostal muscles swing the ribs up and out, the chest cavity enlarges and air is pulled in. Exhalation is normally passive, just recoil.

## Kids are not small adults

Almost every pediatric airway difference comes from proportion.

- The tongue is proportionally much larger and blocks the airway far more easily.
- The occiput (back of the head) is large, so a child lying flat has the neck flexed and the airway kinked. Pad under the shoulders, never under the head.
- The narrowest point is the cricoid ring until about age `8-10`, not the vocal cords.
- The epiglottis is floppier and sits higher. The trachea is shorter and softer, so over-extending the neck kinks it shut.
- Infants under about `6 months` breathe almost entirely through the nose. A stuffy nose is a genuine airway emergency. Suction it.
- Ribs are more horizontal and the chest wall is soft, so children depend on the diaphragm. Anything pressing on the belly hurts their breathing.

The consequence that actually matters on a call: children burn oxygen roughly twice as fast per kilogram and store less of it, so they desaturate in seconds rather than minutes.

> **Key:** In a child, a falling heart rate is a hypoxia alarm. Bradycardia in a sick child means oxygenate and ventilate now, not go hunting for a cardiac cause.
keyPoints: The tongue is the most common airway obstruction; lifting the jaw lifts the tongue.
Adults narrow at the vocal cords; children narrow at the cricoid ring until about age 8-10.
The right mainstem bronchus is straighter, so aspirated material lands in the right lung.
A large occiput flexes a supine child's neck, so pad under the shoulders, not the head.
Children desaturate in seconds and answer hypoxia with bradycardia.

checks.q: You are managing the airway of a 2-year-old lying supine on a backboard. To get a neutral airway position you should:
choices: Place a folded towel under the shoulders
Place a pillow under the head
Hyperextend the neck fully
Turn the head to one side
checks.why: A young child's occiput is proportionally huge, so lying flat already flexes the neck and kinks the airway. Padding under the shoulders restores neutral. A pillow worsens the flexion, and hyperextension kinks a soft trachea shut.

checks.q: An 18-month-old in respiratory distress suddenly drops from a heart rate of 160 to 72. This means:
choices: The child is calming down and improving
A primary cardiac rhythm problem is developing
Severe hypoxia; oxygenate and ventilate immediately
The pulse oximeter probe has slipped
checks.why: Bradycardia in a hypoxic child is a late, ominous sign of profound hypoxia and precedes arrest. It is treated with oxygen and positive pressure ventilation, not with a cardiac workup. Do not interpret a slowing heart rate in a struggling child as improvement.

lessons.title: Adequate or not: reading the breathing
lessons.body:
## Adequate breathing has four parts

Do not ask whether the patient is breathing. Ask whether the breathing is *adequate*, which means four things at once: acceptable rate, acceptable depth, acceptable pattern, acceptable effort.

Normal rates at rest:

| Age | Breaths per minute |
|---|---|
| Adult | 12-20 |
| Child, 1-12 years | 15-30 |
| Infant, under 1 year | 25-50 |

An adult breathing `8` is not moving enough air. An adult breathing `34` shallowly is also not moving enough air, because dead space eats most of it.

Judge depth by watching the chest, not the mouth. You want equal rise on both sides, deep enough to look like a real breath. A patient who can speak a full sentence without stopping is moving air. One answering in two-word bursts is not.

## Work of breathing is the earliest sign

Effort tells you the patient is compensating before any number changes.

- Accessory muscles: neck and shoulder muscles pulling with every breath
- Retractions: skin sucking in between the ribs, above the collarbones, below the sternum. The most reliable pediatric sign.
- Nasal flaring and head bobbing in infants
- Tripod position: sitting up, leaning forward, hands on knees
- Grunting: an infant generating their own back-pressure. Treat it as a red flag.
- Seesaw breathing: belly and chest moving in opposite directions

## What the sounds mean

| Sound | Where | What it means | First move |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snoring | Upper | Tongue falling back | Reposition, adjunct |
| Gurgling | Upper | Fluid, blood, vomit | Suction |
| Stridor | Upper | Narrowing above the cords: croup, epiglottitis, anaphylaxis, foreign body | Keep calm, oxygen, rapid transport |
| Wheezes | Lower | Bronchioles constricted: asthma, COPD, bronchiolitis | Bronchodilator per protocol |
| Crackles or rales | Alveoli | Fluid in the air sacs: heart failure, pneumonia | Sit up, oxygen, consider CPAP |
| Rhonchi | Larger airways | Mucus and secretions | Cough, suction |

> **Trap:** A quiet chest in a known asthmatic is not improvement. No air moving makes no wheeze. A silent chest plus an exhausted patient is someone about to arrest.

## Hypoxia: early looks like anxiety, late looks calm

Early hypoxia is a fight. Restlessness, anxiety, irritability, fast breathing, fast heart rate, slightly elevated blood pressure, pale cool sweaty skin.

Late hypoxia is surrender. Sleepiness, confusion, a slowing heart rate, falling blood pressure, cyanosis, gasping or agonal breathing.

Cyanosis, the blue-gray color, is a *late* sign. Central cyanosis of the lips, tongue and trunk is far more serious than blue fingertips, which can simply be cold.

> **Trap:** Pulse oximetry lies in three common ways. Carbon monoxide poisoning reads falsely high because the meter cannot tell CO from oxygen. Shock, cold fingers and nail polish read falsely low or give no reading at all. Treat the patient, not the number.
keyPoints: Adequate breathing means acceptable rate, depth, pattern and effort, all four at once.
Normal rates: adult 12-20, child 15-30, infant 25-50.
Snoring means reposition, gurgling means suction, stridor is upper airway, wheezes are lower airway, crackles are fluid in alveoli.
Early hypoxia looks anxious and fast; late hypoxia looks sleepy, slow and blue.
A silent chest in an asthmatic and a falsely high SpO2 in CO poisoning are both traps.

checks.q: A 24-year-old asthmatic was wheezing loudly on your arrival. Ten minutes later the wheezing has nearly stopped and he can barely keep his eyes open. This indicates:
choices: The bronchodilator is working and he is tired from the effort
Worsening obstruction with almost no air movement; prepare to ventilate
An anxiety component that has now resolved
A pneumothorax on the left side
checks.why: Wheezing requires moving air. Loss of wheeze plus a deteriorating mental status means the patient is no longer moving enough air to make noise. This is impending respiratory arrest and calls for positive pressure ventilation, not reassurance.

checks.q: Which finding is the earliest reliable sign of hypoxia in an adult?
choices: Central cyanosis of the lips
Bradycardia
Restlessness and anxiety with a rising heart rate
Hypotension
checks.why: Early hypoxia drives a compensatory response: restlessness, anxiety, tachypnea and tachycardia. Cyanosis, bradycardia and hypotension are all late findings that appear once compensation is failing.

checks.q: A patient pulled from a house fire has an SpO2 of 99% on room air but is confused and has a headache. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Carbon monoxide poisoning giving a falsely high SpO2
The patient is fine and the confusion is from stress
A cold probe reading falsely high
The patient has COPD
checks.why: A standard pulse oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so CO poisoning produces a normal or high reading in a severely hypoxic patient. Cold and poor perfusion make readings falsely low, not high.

lessons.title: Opening and clearing the airway
lessons.body:
## Position first, tools second

An unresponsive patient's airway usually closes for one reason: the tongue drops back against the throat. Lifting the jaw forward drags the tongue with it.

**Head-tilt chin-lift** is the default when nothing suggests a spinal injury. One hand on the forehead tilts the head back, the fingers of the other hand lift the bony part of the chin. Do not press the soft tissue under the chin, because that pushes the tongue up.

**Jaw thrust** is the maneuver when mechanism suggests a spine injury: falls, diving, car crashes, any unwitnessed unresponsive trauma. Stand at the head, fingers behind the angles of the jaw, push the jaw forward without moving the neck.

> **Key:** If the jaw thrust does not open the airway, open the airway anyway. A patent airway outranks a theoretical spinal injury. You cannot protect a spine in a patient who is not breathing.

**Recovery position**, rolled onto their side and usually the left, is for an unresponsive patient who is breathing adequately, has no trauma and no reason to stay supine. Gravity drains vomit and secretions out instead of in.

## Suction

You cannot ventilate through fluid, and pushing a bag of air into a mouth full of vomit drives that vomit into the lungs. Suction comes before the bag.

Two tips do two different jobs:

- **Rigid, called a Yankauer or tonsil tip.** The workhorse for the mouth. Big bore, handles vomit, blood and chunks. Only use it where you can see.
- **Soft French catheter.** Flexible and small bore. Used in the nose, down a nasal airway, through a tracheostomy or an endotracheal tube. It clogs on anything thick.

Technique in order:

1. Oxygenate first if the situation allows it.
2. Measure: insert no deeper than the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, the same landmark as an oral airway.
3. Insert with the suction turned **off**.
4. Apply suction while withdrawing, sweeping side to side.
5. Oxygenate again.

Time limits, and they are exam favorites:

| Patient | Maximum per attempt |
|---|---|
| Adult | 15 seconds |
| Child | 10 seconds |
| Infant | 5 seconds |

> **Trap:** Suctioning too long or too deep does two bad things at once. It removes oxygen along with the fluid, and touching the back of the throat stimulates the vagus nerve, which slows the heart. If the heart rate drops, stop and ventilate.

A mounted or portable unit should pull at least `300 mmHg` of vacuum when you clamp the tubing. If the patient is producing vomit faster than you can clear it, log-roll them onto their side and suction with the rigid tip while gravity helps you.
keyPoints: Head-tilt chin-lift is default; jaw thrust when a spine injury is suspected.
If jaw thrust fails to open the airway, use head-tilt chin-lift anyway. Airway wins.
Rigid Yankauer for the mouth and thick material; soft French catheter for the nose, adjuncts and tubes.
Measure corner of mouth to earlobe, insert with suction off, suction on the way out.
Suction no longer than 15 seconds adult, 10 seconds child, 5 seconds infant.

checks.q: You are suctioning vomit from an unresponsive adult. You have been suctioning for 15 seconds and the mouth still is not clear. You should:
choices: Continue until the airway is completely clear
Stop, ventilate and oxygenate, then resume for another 15 seconds
Switch to a soft French catheter and continue
Insert an oral airway and ventilate through the vomit
checks.why: Suctioning removes oxygen as well as fluid and can trigger vagal bradycardia. Break at 15 seconds in an adult, oxygenate or ventilate, then go back. A soft catheter clogs on vomit, and ventilating through vomit drives it into the lungs.

checks.q: An unresponsive patient found at the bottom of a staircase has snoring respirations. You apply a jaw thrust and the snoring continues with no chest rise. Your next action is:
choices: Maintain the jaw thrust and accept the airway as it is
Apply a cervical collar first and reassess
Perform a head-tilt chin-lift to open the airway
Begin chest compressions
checks.why: An unopened airway is fatal within minutes; a spinal cord injury from careful head-tilt is a remote risk. Guidelines are explicit that if a jaw thrust fails, you move to head-tilt chin-lift. A collar does nothing for a closed airway.

lessons.title: Airway adjuncts: the OPA and the NPA
lessons.body:
## Two pieces of plastic, two different jobs

Airway adjuncts hold the tongue off the back of the throat so your positioning does not have to be perfect for the next twenty minutes. Neither one is a definitive airway. Neither seals the trachea, and neither stops vomit from reaching the lungs.

## Oropharyngeal airway, the OPA

A curved plastic tube that lies over the tongue with a flange resting against the lips.

**Sizing.** Measure from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or from the center of the teeth to the angle of the jaw. Too short and it pushes the tongue backward. Too long and it can press the epiglottis down over the airway.

**Insertion in an adult.** Slide it in upside down, tip toward the roof of the mouth, and rotate it `180` degrees as it passes the soft palate. A sideways `90` degree insertion with rotation works equally well.

**Insertion in a child or infant.** Do **not** rotate. Their palate is soft and rotating tears it. Depress the tongue with a tongue blade and insert the airway right side up, following its natural curve.

**Contraindication.** An intact gag reflex. If the patient gags, retches or fights it, pull it out immediately, roll them onto their side, and have suction already running.

> **On the exam:** The OPA is for unresponsive patients with no gag reflex. Any answer choice that puts an OPA in a patient who is groaning, gagging or protecting their own airway is the wrong answer.

## Nasopharyngeal airway, the NPA

A soft rubber tube that passes through a nostril and ends behind the tongue. Its advantage is that most patients tolerate it even with a gag reflex, which makes it the adjunct for a semi-conscious overdose, a postictal seizure patient, or a clenched jaw.

**Sizing.** Length is nostril to earlobe. Diameter should be the largest that fits the nostril without blanching it; the patient's little finger is a rough guide.

**Insertion.** Lubricate generously with water-soluble jelly, never petroleum jelly. Insert into the right nostril with the **bevel toward the septum**, the wall between the nostrils. Advance straight back along the floor of the nasal cavity. Never angle it upward, because there is nothing up there but bone. If it will not pass, do not force it. Try the other nostril, inverting the tube, or drop a size.

**Contraindications.** Suspected basilar skull fracture and severe midface trauma. The fracture line runs through the base of the skull, and a tube pushed straight back can end up inside the cranium.

Findings that should stop you: bruising around both eyes (raccoon eyes), bruising behind the ear (Battle sign), and clear or blood-tinged fluid draining from the nose or ears.

> **Trap:** A minor nosebleed after NPA insertion is common and is usually not a reason to pull it. Remove it and you often end up with an obstructed airway plus a bleeding nose.
keyPoints: OPA sizing is corner of the mouth to the earlobe; NPA sizing is nostril to earlobe.
Rotate an OPA 180 degrees in adults; never rotate in children, use a tongue blade instead.
An OPA is contraindicated with any gag reflex; remove it immediately if the patient gags.
NPA goes in bevel toward the septum, lubricated, straight back along the floor of the nose.
NPA is contraindicated with suspected basilar skull fracture or severe midface trauma.

checks.q: A 30-year-old is unresponsive after a heroin overdose, breathing 8 times a minute, and gags when you attempt an oral airway. The correct adjunct is:
choices: A smaller oral airway inserted sideways
A nasopharyngeal airway sized nostril to earlobe
No adjunct at all; just ventilate
An oral airway inserted without rotation
checks.why: An intact gag reflex rules out any oral airway regardless of size or technique. The NPA is designed for exactly this patient and is usually tolerated. Skipping the adjunct entirely leaves the tongue obstructing during ventilation.

checks.q: An unresponsive patient struck in the face has raccoon eyes and clear fluid from the left ear. Which airway is contraindicated?
choices: Oropharyngeal airway
Bag-valve mask ventilation
Nasopharyngeal airway
Head-tilt chin-lift positioning
checks.why: Raccoon eyes and clear otorrhea suggest a basilar skull fracture, so nothing goes in the nose: an NPA can be pushed through the fracture into the cranium. The OPA and bag-valve mask remain appropriate in an unresponsive patient without a gag reflex.

lessons.title: Oxygen delivery devices and their numbers
lessons.body:
## Start from what room air already gives you

Room air is `21%` oxygen. Everything below is about adding to that, and about whether the patient is moving enough air for the extra oxygen to reach anything.

| Device | Flow | Delivered oxygen | Use it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nasal cannula | 1-6 L/min | 24-44% | Mild hypoxia, cannot tolerate a mask |
| Simple face mask | 6-10 L/min | 35-60% | Moderate need, a middle step |
| Nonrebreather mask | 10-15 L/min | up to 90% | Serious hypoxia, breathing adequately |
| Bag-valve mask with reservoir | 15 L/min | near 100% | Inadequate or absent breathing |

## Nasal cannula

Two prongs in the nostrils. Each added liter per minute raises delivered oxygen by roughly `4%` over room air, which is where `24-44%` comes from.

Above `6 L/min` it dries and burns the nasal lining without delivering meaningfully more. If a cannula at `6 L/min` is not enough, change the device. Do not just crank the flow.

## Simple face mask

Covers nose and mouth, has open side ports and no reservoir. It requires a minimum of `6 L/min`, because below that the patient rebreathes their own exhaled carbon dioxide trapped in the mask.

## Nonrebreather

A mask with a reservoir bag and one-way valves. The patient inhales from the bag and exhaled air leaves through the side ports without re-entering the reservoir.

Prime the bag before it touches the face: cover the valve until the reservoir fills. Run `10-15 L/min`, high enough that the bag never collapses more than about a third when the patient inhales. A collapsing bag means the flow is too low for that patient's demand.

> **Trap:** A nonrebreather does nothing for a patient who is not moving air. If the tidal volume is poor or the rate is `6`, the right device is a bag-valve mask, not a bigger mask.

## Children and other cases

Small children fight masks, and a screaming child is worse off than a calm one getting `30%` oxygen. Blow-by, meaning oxygen tubing or a mask held a few inches from the face at about `6 L/min`, often by the parent, is a legitimate technique and not a consolation prize.

Humidification is added for long transports and dry-airway complaints such as croup. Dry oxygen thickens secretions, which is exactly what a narrowed airway does not need.

> **Key:** Pick the device from the `SpO2` and the work of breathing, then titrate. Target `94-99%` for most patients and `88-92%` for known COPD. Oxygen is a drug. Too much for too long has its own harms, and too little kills right now.
keyPoints: Room air is 21% oxygen; a nasal cannula adds roughly 4% per liter, giving 24-44% at 1-6 L/min.
Simple mask needs at least 6 L/min to flush exhaled CO2; it delivers 35-60% at 6-10 L/min.
Nonrebreather runs 10-15 L/min for up to 90%, and the reservoir must stay at least two-thirds inflated.
Bag-valve mask with reservoir at 15 L/min delivers near 100% and is the only device that ventilates.
Blow-by at about 6 L/min is the right answer for a child who fights a mask.

checks.q: You apply a nonrebreather at 10 L/min and notice the reservoir bag collapses completely with each breath. You should:
choices: Switch to a nasal cannula at 6 L/min
Increase the flow until the bag stays partly inflated, up to 15 L/min
Remove the mask because it is malfunctioning
Leave it, because a collapsing bag means the patient is getting all the oxygen
checks.why: A fully collapsing reservoir means the patient's inspiratory demand exceeds the flow, so they are drawing room air around the seal. Raise the flow toward 15 L/min. Downgrading the device or removing it gives the hypoxic patient less oxygen, not more.

checks.q: A 70-year-old with COPD has an SpO2 of 85%, speaks in short phrases and has good chest rise. The best initial device is:
choices: Nonrebreather at 15 L/min, titrated down toward 88-92%
Bag-valve mask at 15 L/min
No oxygen, to protect the hypoxic drive
Simple face mask at 4 L/min
checks.why: This patient is hypoxic but still ventilating adequately, so a nonrebreather is correct and the target is 88-92% for COPD. A bag-valve mask is for inadequate ventilation. A simple mask at 4 L/min is below its 6 L/min minimum and causes rebreathing.

lessons.title: Oxygen cylinders, safety and the duration math
lessons.body:
## What is in the tank

Medical oxygen is stored as a compressed gas in steel or aluminum cylinders, marked green in the United States. A full cylinder reads about `2,000 psi` on the regulator gauge; some newer cylinders fill to `2,200 psi`.

| Cylinder | Approximate capacity | Where you find it |
|---|---|---|
| D | 350 L | Jump bag, portable |
| E | 625 L | Stretcher-mounted portable |
| M | 3,000 L | On-board main supply |
| H or K | 6,900 L | Fixed installation |

`200 psi` is the **safe residual pressure**. At or below that, the gauge stops being trustworthy and the delivered flow falls off. Swap the cylinder. Do not run one to zero.

## The duration formula

You will be asked to calculate this on the exam.

`(gauge pressure in psi minus 200) x constant / flow rate in L/min = minutes remaining`

The constants are worth memorizing cold:

- D = `0.16`
- E = `0.28`
- M = `1.56`

**Example 1.** A D cylinder reads `1,600 psi` and you are running a nonrebreather at `15 L/min`. `1600 - 200 = 1400`. `1400 x 0.16 = 224`. `224 / 15 = 14.9`, about `15 minutes`.

**Example 2.** A full E cylinder at `2,000 psi`, nonrebreather at `15 L/min`. `1800 x 0.28 = 504`. `504 / 15 = 33.6`, about `34 minutes`.

**Example 3.** The same E cylinder at `1,000 psi` running a cannula at `6 L/min`. `800 x 0.28 = 224`. `224 / 6 = 37 minutes`.

> **On the exam:** The first mistake they are testing is forgetting to subtract `200`. The second is using the wrong constant. Write the formula and the three constants on your scratch paper before the test starts.

## Handling it safely

Oxygen does not burn. It makes everything else burn violently, and a compressed cylinder stores an enormous amount of mechanical energy.

- Keep oil, grease, petroleum jelly and adhesive residue away from cylinders, regulators and fittings. Oxygen under pressure plus a hydrocarbon can ignite with no spark at all.
- Never let a cylinder stand unsecured. If it falls and the valve stem snaps, the cylinder becomes a projectile that goes through walls.
- Open the valve slowly and fully, then back it off a quarter turn so the next person can tell it is open.
- Use the correct pin-index yoke and a fresh gasket. Never force a fitting or stack washers to stop a leak.
- Keep cylinders below `125` degrees Fahrenheit and out of direct sun.
- Cylinders are hydrostatically tested every `5` years and the date is stamped on the shoulder.

> **On shift:** Check the gauge at the start of every shift and check it again before committing to a long transport at high flow. A nonrebreather empties a D cylinder in roughly fifteen minutes.
keyPoints: A full cylinder is about 2,000 psi and the safe residual is 200 psi.
Duration formula: (psi minus 200) x constant / flow = minutes remaining.
No oil, grease or petroleum products near oxygen equipment, and always secure the cylinder.
Cylinders are hydrostatically tested every 5 years and stored below 125 degrees Fahrenheit.

checks.q: An E cylinder reads 1,600 psi and you are running a nonrebreather at 12 L/min. Approximately how long until you reach safe residual?
choices: About 33 minutes
About 37 minutes
About 19 minutes
About 45 minutes
checks.why: 1600 minus 200 is 1400. 1400 times the E constant of 0.28 equals 392. 392 divided by 12 equals about 33 minutes. Forgetting to subtract 200 gives about 37 minutes, and using the D constant gives about 19.

checks.q: Why is petroleum jelly kept away from oxygen regulators?
choices: It clogs the pin-index holes
It degrades the rubber gasket over time
It reacts with oxygen and can ignite spontaneously under pressure
It falsely raises the pressure gauge reading
checks.why: High-pressure oxygen plus a hydrocarbon can auto-ignite without any spark or flame, which is why no oil, grease or petroleum product touches oxygen equipment. The other options are not the safety hazard being tested.

lessons.title: Ventilating: the bag-valve mask and the rates
lessons.body:
## When a mask is not enough

Positive pressure ventilation means you are pushing air in, not just enriching what the patient pulls in on their own. You do it when the patient is not moving enough air:

- No breathing at all, or only agonal gasps
- An adult rate under about `10` or over about `30` with poor chest rise
- Chest rise that is barely visible at any rate
- Cyanosis or an `SpO2` that will not come up on high-flow oxygen
- Altered mental status caused by the hypoxia itself

## Holding the mask is the hard part

The bag is easy. The seal is where ventilation fails.

**One rescuer, the C-E grip.** Thumb and index finger form a C on the mask body, pressing it down. The other three fingers form an E along the bony ridge of the jaw, lifting the jaw *up into the mask*. You are pulling the face into the mask, not mashing the mask onto the face. Squeeze the bag against your forearm or thigh.

**Two rescuers, always better.** One provider uses both hands, a C-E grip on each side, and holds the head in position. The second squeezes the bag. Measured tidal volumes are substantially higher this way. If you have the people, use them.

Adult bags hold `1,200-1,600 mL`. You are not delivering all of it. Squeeze only until the chest visibly rises, over about `1 second`.

## The rates, memorized

| Situation | Rate |
|---|---|
| Adult with a pulse | 1 breath every 6 seconds, 10 per minute |
| Child or infant with a pulse | 1 breath every 2-3 seconds, 20-30 per minute |
| CPR, no advanced airway | 30:2, breaths delivered in the pause |
| CPR, advanced airway in place | 1 breath every 6 seconds, compressions never stop |

> **Trap:** Bagging too fast or too hard is one of the most common errors in EMS. It raises pressure inside the chest, which chokes off blood returning to the heart and drops cardiac output. Count out loud: squeeze, two, three, four, five, six.

## Air in the stomach

Excess volume and excess speed force air past the esophagus into the stomach. A distended stomach shoves the diaphragm upward, makes ventilation harder, and eventually produces vomit and aspiration.

Prevention is technique: good head position, slow gentle squeezes, chest rise only. Cricoid pressure, the Sellick maneuver, is **no longer recommended**. It does not reliably prevent aspiration and it can deform and obstruct the airway.

## Special anatomy

A patient with a **stoma** or tracheostomy breathes through a hole in the neck. Ventilate through the stoma with an infant or child mask sealed over it, or attach the bag directly to the `15 mm` adapter on a trach tube. If air escapes from the mouth and nose, seal them, because that patient has a partial laryngectomy.

A **pocket mask** with a one-way valve and oxygen at `15 L/min` delivers roughly `50-55%` and often achieves better volumes than one-rescuer bagging, because both of your hands are on the seal.

Signs it is working: visible chest rise, improving color, a rising `SpO2`, a heart rate coming back toward normal. Signs it is not: no chest rise, a growing belly, falling saturation.
keyPoints: Ventilate an adult with a pulse once every 6 seconds; a child or infant once every 2-3 seconds.
With an advanced airway during CPR it is 1 breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions.
Squeeze only to visible chest rise, over about 1 second, to avoid gastric inflation.
Two-rescuer bag-valve mask with two C-E grips beats one-rescuer technique every time.
Cricoid pressure is no longer recommended, and hyperventilation drops cardiac output.

checks.q: You are ventilating an apneic adult who has a strong carotid pulse. The correct rate is:
choices: 1 breath every 3 seconds
1 breath every 6 seconds
1 breath every 10 seconds
As fast as you can squeeze the bag
checks.why: An adult with a pulse gets 1 breath every 6 seconds, or 10 per minute. Every 3 seconds is the pediatric rate and would hyperventilate an adult, raising intrathoracic pressure and reducing venous return. Every 10 seconds under-ventilates.

checks.q: Midway through bagging, the patient's abdomen is visibly distending and chest rise is decreasing. The most likely cause is:
choices: The oxygen flow rate is too low
The mask is the wrong size
Internal bleeding in the abdomen
Squeezing too fast and too forcefully, forcing air into the stomach
checks.why: Rapid, high-pressure squeezes push air past the esophagus into the stomach, which then splints the diaphragm and reduces chest rise. Slow down, squeeze over one second to chest rise only, and recheck head position. Oxygen flow does not cause gastric distention.

checks.q: A patient with a permanent laryngectomy stoma requires ventilation. You should:
choices: Ventilate through the mouth with a good mask seal
Seal an infant or child mask over the stoma and ventilate there
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway first
Perform a head-tilt chin-lift and ventilate normally
checks.why: The stoma is the airway in a laryngectomy patient; the mouth and nose no longer connect to the trachea. Use a small mask sealed over the stoma or attach the bag to the trach tube's 15 mm adapter. Positioning maneuvers do not help.

lessons.title: CPAP: pressure, not oxygen
lessons.body:
## What CPAP actually does

CPAP stands for continuous positive airway pressure. A tight mask and a flow generator hold a constant back-pressure in the airway through the entire breathing cycle, on the way in and on the way out.

That constant pressure does four useful things:

1. It splints open alveoli and small airways that would otherwise collapse at the end of each breath, so more surface is available for gas exchange.
2. In heart failure, it physically pushes fluid out of the alveoli back into the capillaries.
3. It reduces preload and afterload, which unloads a failing left ventricle.
4. It takes over part of the work of breathing so an exhausted patient can rest.

> **Key:** CPAP is not oxygen. It is pressure. It is the single intervention most likely to keep a pulmonary edema patient off a ventilator.

## Who gets it

The patient must be **awake, breathing on their own, and able to follow instructions**. Typical triggers are a respiratory rate over `25`, an `SpO2` under `94%` despite oxygen, accessory muscle use, and a patient who is obviously working hard.

The conditions with the best evidence and the widest protocol support are acute heart failure with pulmonary edema, COPD exacerbation, asthma, near-drowning, and pneumonia with hypoxia.

## Who does not

- Apnea, agonal breathing or respiratory arrest. These patients need a bag, not a pressure they cannot use.
- Unable to follow commands or protect the airway
- Hypotension, generally a systolic under `90 mmHg`. The raised pressure inside the chest reduces venous return and can drop the pressure further.
- Suspected pneumothorax or penetrating chest trauma
- Major facial trauma, facial burns, or any face the mask cannot seal
- Active vomiting or upper gastrointestinal bleeding
- Tracheostomy

## Running it

Start around `5 cmH2O` and titrate up toward `10 cmH2O` as the patient tolerates it and protocol allows. Most services cap EMT-level CPAP in that `5-10` range.

The failure mode is almost never the machine. It is the patient. The mask feels like leaning out the window of a moving car. Hold the mask against the face by hand first so they feel the flow, then strap it on. Keep talking: tell them what it feels like, that it gets easier, that you are staying right there. Coaching is the skill.

Check a blood pressure before you start and every `5 minutes` after.

> **Trap:** Deterioration on CPAP is not a reason to turn the pressure up. If the patient gets sleepy, the systolic falls, they vomit, or they are simply no better after a good trial, take it off and ventilate with a bag-valve mask. Nobody should die with a CPAP mask strapped to their face.

Whether an EMT may apply CPAP, and at what pressures, varies by protocol and state. In New Jersey it is an authorized EMT skill under standing orders in most regions. Know the protocol you work under.
keyPoints: CPAP delivers constant pressure through the whole cycle: it recruits alveoli, pushes edema fluid back, and drops preload and afterload.
The patient must be awake, breathing on their own, and able to follow commands.
Typical settings are 5-10 cmH2O, started low and titrated up.
Contraindications: apnea, cannot protect the airway, systolic under 90, pneumothorax, facial trauma, vomiting.
Falling mental status, falling pressure or vomiting means remove CPAP and bag the patient.

checks.q: A 68-year-old in pulmonary edema is on CPAP at 10 cmH2O. Over five minutes his systolic falls from 132 to 84 and he becomes drowsy. You should:
choices: Increase the pressure to 15 cmH2O
Remove CPAP and ventilate with a bag-valve mask
Leave CPAP on and give a fluid bolus
Reduce the oxygen concentration and continue
checks.why: Hypotension and a falling mental status are both stop signs. The intrathoracic pressure is cutting venous return, and a drowsy patient can no longer protect the airway. Remove the mask and ventilate. Raising the pressure worsens both problems.

checks.q: Which patient is the best candidate for CPAP?
choices: An unresponsive overdose breathing 6 times a minute
A hypotensive trauma patient with a suspected pneumothorax
An alert 74-year-old with crackles, an SpO2 of 86%, a rate of 30, and a blood pressure of 160/94
A patient in cardiac arrest with an AED attached
checks.why: CPAP requires an awake, spontaneously breathing patient who can follow commands, and pulmonary edema is its best indication. The overdose and the arrest patient need ventilation. Hypotension and pneumothorax are both absolute contraindications.

lessons.title: Choking, difficult airways and working with ALS
lessons.body:
## Mild versus severe obstruction

Someone choking either can move air or cannot, and that single distinction decides everything.

**Mild, or partial.** Forceful cough, able to speak or cry, wheezing between coughs, still pink. Do nothing invasive. Encourage coughing, because a cough generates more pressure than anything you can do by hand. Stay close, give oxygen, transport. Slapping the back of a partially obstructed patient can convert it to a complete obstruction.

**Severe, or complete.** Silent or weak cough, unable to speak or cry, high-pitched stridor or no sound at all, hands clutching the throat, which is the universal choking sign, and a patient turning blue. Act now.

## What to do, by age

**Adult or child over `1` year, responsive.** Abdominal thrusts. Stand behind the patient, place a fist thumb-side in just above the navel and well below the sternum, grasp it with the other hand, and deliver quick inward and upward thrusts. Repeat until the object comes out or the patient goes unresponsive. Use **chest thrusts** instead if the patient is visibly pregnant or too large to reach around.

**Infant under `1` year, responsive.** Hold the infant face down along your forearm with the head lower than the body, supporting the jaw. Deliver `5` back slaps between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Flip face up and deliver `5` chest thrusts with two fingers on the lower half of the sternum, the same landmark as compressions. Repeat the cycle. No abdominal thrusts on infants, because the liver sits unprotected below a soft rib cage.

**Anyone who goes unresponsive, any age.** Lower them to the ground and start CPR beginning with chest compressions. The compressions themselves generate airway pressure.

> **Key:** Each time you open the airway to deliver a breath, look in the mouth. Remove an object only if you can actually see it. Never perform a blind finger sweep. It pushes objects deeper and it is a wrong answer on every version of this exam.

## Airways with complications

**Dentures.** Leave well-fitting dentures in place, because they give the face structure and improve your mask seal. Remove partials or broken plates that have come loose.

**Facial trauma.** Expect blood, swelling and distorted anatomy. Suction aggressively with the rigid tip, position to drain, and anticipate a difficult bag-valve mask seal. Severe midface trauma rules out a nasal airway.

**Laryngectomy.** The patient breathes through a neck stoma. Ventilate the stoma, not the mouth.

## Working with ALS

**Supraglottic airways**, devices such as the King LT, the i-gel or a laryngeal mask, are blind-insertion tubes that seat above the vocal cords and block the esophagus. Some states, including parts of New Jersey, permit EMTs to place them under protocol, and many do not. They never substitute for good bag-valve mask technique.

**Assisting with intubation.** Preoxygenate for at least `30 seconds` before the attempt, keep working suction in your hand, pass equipment as asked, and call out if the `SpO2` falls. Apply cricoid pressure only if specifically requested, because it is no longer routine.

Confirmation is **waveform capnography**. A continuous square `ETCO2` waveform is the gold standard for a tube in the trachea, and it is the first thing to vanish when the tube is displaced during a move.
keyPoints: Mild obstruction: encourage coughing and do not intervene. Severe: act immediately.
Abdominal thrusts for adults and children over 1; back slaps and chest thrusts, 5 and 5, for infants.
Any choking patient who becomes unresponsive gets CPR, starting with compressions.
Look in the mouth before each breath and remove only what you can see. No blind finger sweeps.
Waveform capnography is the gold standard for confirming and monitoring an endotracheal tube.

checks.q: An 8-month-old is choking, silent, and turning blue. The correct sequence is:
choices: Abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled
5 back slaps followed by 5 chest thrusts, repeated
A blind finger sweep, then rescue breaths
Two rescue breaths, then 30 compressions
checks.why: Infants get alternating cycles of 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts because abdominal thrusts can lacerate an unprotected liver. Blind finger sweeps drive objects deeper, and CPR is reserved for the moment the infant becomes unresponsive.

checks.q: A paramedic has just intubated your patient. The best confirmation that the tube is in the trachea is:
choices: Misting inside the tube
Equal chest rise
A continuous waveform capnography tracing
Absence of sounds over the stomach
checks.why: Waveform capnography is the gold standard and also monitors continuously for displacement. Tube misting is unreliable, and chest rise and epigastric auscultation are supportive findings that can all be present with a misplaced tube.

cards.front: What is the difference between ventilation, oxygenation and respiration?
cards.back: Ventilation is air moving in and out. Oxygenation is oxygen loading onto hemoglobin. Respiration is gas exchange at the cell. Each can fail separately.

cards.front: How do you calculate minute volume, and what is a normal adult value?
cards.back: Minute volume = tidal volume x respiratory rate. Adult: about 500 mL x 12-20, so roughly 6,000-10,000 mL per minute.

cards.front: How much of each adult breath is dead space, and why does it matter?
cards.back: About 150 mL sits in the mouth, trachea and bronchi and never reaches an alveolus. It is wasted on every breath, so shallow fast breathing wastes most of the minute volume.

cards.front: Why can high-flow oxygen raise CO2 in a COPD patient, and does that mean withhold it?
cards.back: Mostly V/Q mismatch plus the Haldane effect, not loss of hypoxic drive. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient. Give it and titrate.

cards.front: What SpO2 target do you use for a COPD patient versus everyone else?
cards.back: COPD: 88-92%. Most other patients: 94-99%. Do not chase 100%.

cards.front: Which device fixes an oxygenation problem and which fixes a ventilation problem?
cards.back: Oxygen masks fix oxygenation. Only positive pressure from a bag-valve mask or pocket mask fixes inadequate ventilation.

cards.front: Name the three sections of the pharynx from top down.
cards.back: Nasopharynx behind the nose, oropharynx behind the mouth, laryngopharynx where the tube splits into trachea and esophagus.

cards.front: What is the narrowest point of the airway in an adult and in a young child?
cards.back: Adult: the space between the vocal cords. Child under about 8-10 years: the cricoid ring below the cords.

cards.front: Why do aspirated objects and over-inserted tubes end up in the right lung?
cards.back: The right mainstem bronchus leaves the carina at a straighter, less angled path than the left, so anything falling down the trachea goes right.

cards.front: Why do you pad under a small child's shoulders instead of under the head?
cards.back: Their occiput is proportionally large, so lying flat already flexes the neck and kinks the airway. Shoulder padding restores a neutral position.

cards.front: Why is a blocked nose an airway emergency in an infant under 6 months?
cards.back: Infants that age breathe almost entirely through the nose and do not reliably switch to mouth breathing. Suction the nares.

cards.front: Why do children desaturate so much faster than adults?
cards.back: They consume oxygen roughly twice as fast per kilogram and hold less reserve volume in smaller lungs, so seconds of apnea drop the saturation.

cards.front: What does a falling heart rate mean in a child with respiratory distress?
cards.back: Severe hypoxia. Bradycardia is a pediatric hypoxia alarm and precedes arrest. Oxygenate and ventilate immediately.

cards.front: What are normal resting respiratory rates for an adult, a child and an infant?
cards.back: Adult 12-20, child aged 1-12 years 15-30, infant under 1 year 25-50 breaths per minute.

cards.front: Stridor: where is the problem and what causes it?
cards.back: Upper airway narrowing above the cords. Causes include croup, epiglottitis, anaphylaxis and a foreign body. Keep the patient calm, give oxygen, transport fast.

cards.front: Wheezing: where is the problem and what is the fix?
cards.back: Lower airway. Constricted bronchioles from asthma, COPD or bronchiolitis. Treat with a bronchodilator per protocol plus oxygen.

cards.front: Crackles, also called rales: what do they mean?
cards.back: Fluid in the alveoli, usually heart failure or pneumonia. Sit the patient up, give oxygen, consider CPAP.

cards.front: What do snoring and gurgling each tell you to do?
cards.back: Snoring means the tongue is falling back, so reposition and place an adjunct. Gurgling means fluid, so suction immediately.

cards.front: List the early signs of hypoxia in an adult.
cards.back: Restlessness, anxiety, irritability, fast breathing, fast heart rate, slightly elevated blood pressure, pale cool sweaty skin.

cards.front: List the late signs of hypoxia.
cards.back: Sleepiness, confusion, slowing heart rate, falling blood pressure, cyanosis, and gasping or agonal breathing.

cards.front: Why is a silent chest in a known asthmatic worse than loud wheezing?
cards.back: Wheezing requires air movement. A silent chest means almost nothing is moving. Silent chest plus exhaustion equals impending respiratory arrest.

cards.front: Name three situations where pulse oximetry misleads you.
cards.back: Carbon monoxide poisoning reads falsely high. Shock and cold extremities read falsely low. Nail polish or dirt can block the reading entirely.

cards.front: When do you use head-tilt chin-lift versus jaw thrust?
cards.back: Head-tilt chin-lift when there is no suspicion of spinal injury. Jaw thrust when mechanism suggests a spine injury, because it opens the airway without moving the neck.

cards.front: The jaw thrust fails to open a trauma patient's airway. Now what?
cards.back: Use head-tilt chin-lift anyway. A patent airway outranks a possible spinal injury; you cannot protect a spine in a patient who is not breathing.

cards.front: Who goes in the recovery position, and why?
cards.back: An unresponsive patient breathing adequately with no trauma. Lying on the side lets gravity drain vomit and secretions out of the airway instead of into the lungs.

cards.front: Rigid Yankauer versus soft French catheter: when do you use each?
cards.back: Rigid for the mouth and thick material like vomit, blood and chunks, under direct vision. Soft for the nose, through an NPA, or down a trach or ET tube.

cards.front: How deep do you insert a suction catheter, and when do you apply suction?
cards.back: No deeper than corner of the mouth to earlobe. Insert with suction off, then apply suction only while withdrawing, sweeping side to side.

cards.front: What are the maximum suction times for an adult, a child and an infant?
cards.back: Adult 15 seconds, child 10 seconds, infant 5 seconds per attempt. Oxygenate before and after each attempt.

cards.front: Why can suctioning cause bradycardia?
cards.back: Touching the back of the throat stimulates the vagus nerve, which slows the heart. It also removes oxygen. If the rate drops, stop and ventilate.

cards.front: How do you size an oropharyngeal airway?
cards.back: Corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or center of the teeth to the angle of the jaw. Too long can press the epiglottis over the airway.

cards.front: How does OPA insertion differ between an adult and a child?
cards.back: Adult: insert upside down and rotate 180 degrees, or sideways and rotate 90. Child or infant: never rotate. Depress the tongue with a blade and insert right side up.

cards.front: What is the contraindication to an OPA, and what do you do if it happens?
cards.back: An intact gag reflex. If the patient gags or retches, remove it immediately, roll them onto their side, and suction.

cards.front: How do you size a nasopharyngeal airway?
cards.back: Length is nostril to earlobe. Diameter is the largest that fits the nostril without blanching it; the patient's little finger is a rough guide.

cards.front: Describe correct NPA insertion.
cards.back: Lubricate with water-soluble jelly, insert into the right nostril with the bevel toward the septum, and advance straight back along the floor of the nose. Never angle upward.

cards.front: What are the contraindications to an NPA, and which findings suggest them?
cards.back: Suspected basilar skull fracture and severe midface trauma. Look for raccoon eyes, Battle sign behind the ear, and clear or bloody fluid from the nose or ears.

cards.front: Do airway adjuncts protect against aspiration?
cards.back: No. Neither an OPA nor an NPA seals the trachea. They only hold the tongue forward. Keep suction ready regardless.

cards.front: Nasal cannula: what flow range and what delivered oxygen?
cards.back: 1-6 L/min delivering about 24-44%, roughly 4% more per liter above room air. Above 6 L/min it only dries the nose.

cards.front: Simple face mask: what flow and why is there a minimum?
cards.back: 6-10 L/min delivering about 35-60%. Below 6 L/min the patient rebreathes exhaled carbon dioxide trapped inside the mask.

cards.front: Nonrebreather: what flow, what concentration, and what must the reservoir do?
cards.back: 10-15 L/min, up to about 90%. Prime the bag before applying it, and keep flow high enough that the reservoir never collapses more than about a third.

cards.front: What flow rate does a bag-valve mask need, and what does it deliver?
cards.back: 15 L/min with the reservoir attached, delivering near 100%. Without the reservoir it falls to roughly 40-60%.

cards.front: A toddler screams and rips off every mask you try. What do you do?
cards.back: Blow-by: hold oxygen tubing or a mask a few inches from the face at about 6 L/min, ideally in the parent's hand. A calm child on blow-by beats a screaming one on a mask.

cards.front: Why is a nonrebreather the wrong choice for an adult breathing 6 times a minute?
cards.back: That is a ventilation failure, not an oxygenation failure. No mask moves air. The patient needs positive pressure ventilation with a bag-valve mask at 1 breath every 6 seconds.

cards.front: What pressure reads full on an oxygen cylinder, and what is safe residual?
cards.back: Full is about 2,000 psi, up to 2,200 on some cylinders. Safe residual is 200 psi. Change the cylinder at or before 200.

cards.front: What are the cylinder constants for D, E and M tanks?
cards.back: D = 0.16, E = 0.28, M = 1.56. These convert remaining pressure into liters of usable gas.

cards.front: State the oxygen cylinder duration formula.
cards.back: (gauge psi minus 200) x the cylinder constant, divided by the flow rate in L/min, equals minutes of oxygen remaining.

cards.front: A D cylinder reads 1,600 psi and you are running 15 L/min. How long do you have?
cards.back: 1600 minus 200 is 1400. 1400 x 0.16 = 224. 224 divided by 15 is about 15 minutes.

cards.front: A full E cylinder at 2,000 psi runs a nonrebreather at 15 L/min. How long?
cards.back: 1800 x 0.28 = 504. 504 divided by 15 is about 34 minutes.

cards.front: Why is oil or grease dangerous around oxygen equipment?
cards.back: High-pressure oxygen plus a hydrocarbon can ignite spontaneously, with no spark. Keep petroleum products off cylinders, regulators and fittings.

cards.front: List the indications for positive pressure ventilation.
cards.back: Apnea or agonal gasps, an adult rate under 10 or over 30 with poor chest rise, barely visible chest rise, cyanosis or SpO2 that will not rise on high-flow oxygen.

cards.front: Describe the one-rescuer C-E grip.
cards.back: Thumb and index finger make a C pressing the mask down; the other three fingers make an E along the bony jaw, lifting the jaw up into the mask. Lift the face to the mask.

cards.front: Why is two-rescuer bag-valve mask ventilation preferred?
cards.back: One provider uses two hands, a C-E grip on each side, for a far better seal while the second squeezes the bag. Measured tidal volumes are substantially higher.

cards.front: How much volume and how fast do you squeeze a bag-valve mask?
cards.back: Only enough to produce visible chest rise, delivered over about 1 second. Adult bags hold 1,200-1,600 mL and you never deliver all of it.

cards.front: What is the ventilation rate for an adult with a pulse versus a child or infant with a pulse?
cards.back: Adult: 1 breath every 6 seconds, 10 per minute. Child or infant: 1 breath every 2-3 seconds, 20-30 per minute.

cards.front: What is the ventilation rate during CPR once an advanced airway is in place?
cards.back: 1 breath every 6 seconds, 10 per minute, with continuous compressions and no pauses for breaths.

cards.front: Why is hyperventilation harmful, and is cricoid pressure still recommended?
cards.back: Hyperventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, cuts venous return and drops cardiac output. Cricoid pressure is no longer recommended; it can obstruct the airway.

cards.front: How do you ventilate a patient with a tracheostomy or laryngectomy stoma?
cards.back: Seal an infant or child mask over the stoma, or attach the bag to the trach tube's 15 mm adapter. Seal the mouth and nose if air escapes there.

cards.front: By what mechanisms does CPAP help a patient in pulmonary edema?
cards.back: It splints alveoli open, pushes fluid back into the capillaries, reduces preload and afterload, and takes over part of the work of breathing.

cards.front: What three things must be true about a patient before you apply CPAP?
cards.back: Awake, breathing on their own, and able to follow commands. Plus a systolic above 90 and a face the mask can seal.

cards.front: List the main contraindications to CPAP.
cards.back: Apnea or agonal breathing, unable to protect the airway, systolic under 90, suspected pneumothorax or penetrating chest trauma, major facial trauma, active vomiting, tracheostomy.

cards.front: What pressure settings does an EMT typically use for CPAP?
cards.back: Start around 5 cmH2O and titrate up toward 10 cmH2O as tolerated. Most EMT protocols cap it in the 5-10 range. Varies by protocol.

cards.front: When do you take CPAP off?
cards.back: Falling mental status, systolic dropping, vomiting, or no improvement after a good trial. Remove the mask and ventilate with a bag-valve mask instead.

cards.front: How do you tell mild from severe airway obstruction, and what do you do for mild?
cards.back: Mild: forceful cough, can speak, still pink. Encourage coughing, give oxygen, transport. Do not slap the back or do thrusts.

cards.front: What do you do for a severe obstruction in a responsive adult, and what is the alternative technique?
cards.back: Abdominal thrusts, fist just above the navel, quick inward and upward. Use chest thrusts if the patient is visibly pregnant or too large to reach around.

cards.front: What is the sequence for a responsive choking infant?
cards.back: 5 back slaps between the shoulder blades with the head lower than the body, then 5 chest thrusts with two fingers on the lower sternum. Repeat. Never abdominal thrusts.

cards.front: A choking patient goes unresponsive. What is your next action?
cards.back: Lower them to the ground and begin CPR starting with chest compressions. Compressions generate airway pressure that can dislodge the object.

cards.front: When may you remove an object from a choking patient's mouth?
cards.back: Only when you can actually see it. Look in the mouth each time you open the airway for a breath. Never perform a blind finger sweep.

cards.front: What is a supraglottic airway and where does it sit?
cards.back: A blind-insertion device such as a King LT, i-gel or laryngeal mask that seats above the vocal cords and blocks the esophagus. EMT use varies by state and protocol.

cards.front: What are your jobs when assisting a paramedic with intubation?
cards.back: Preoxygenate at least 30 seconds, hold working suction, pass equipment, watch and call out the SpO2, and apply cricoid pressure only if asked.

quiz.q: A patient trapped in a burning building has no burns and is breathing 18 times a minute with good chest rise, yet is unconscious. Which process is primarily impaired?
choices: Ventilation
Oxygenation
Respiration at the cell
Perfusion of the lungs
quiz.why: Air is moving normally, so ventilation is intact. What is missing is oxygen in that air and carbon monoxide competing for hemoglobin, which is an oxygenation failure. Cellular respiration failure describes cyanide, and lung perfusion is not the primary issue here.

quiz.q: Which of the following best defines tidal volume?
choices: The total air the lungs can hold
The air left after a full exhalation
The volume of one normal breath, about 500 mL in an adult
Tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate
quiz.why: Tidal volume is the amount moved in a single normal breath, roughly 500 mL or 5-7 mL/kg. Total capacity and residual volume are different measures, and the last choice describes minute volume.

quiz.q: A 66-year-old with severe COPD has an SpO2 of 79%, is using accessory muscles, and is still alert. What is the correct management?
choices: High-flow oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 88-92%, with a bag-valve mask at hand
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min and nothing more, to preserve the hypoxic drive
No oxygen until you can obtain an end-tidal CO2 reading
Immediate bag-valve mask ventilation at 20 breaths per minute
quiz.why: Hypoxia is the immediate threat and oxygen is never withheld for it; the COPD target is 88-92%. Capping at 2 L/min or waiting for capnography leaves the patient hypoxic. He is still ventilating, so forced ventilation at 20 per minute is premature and would hyperventilate him.

quiz.q: You are managing the airway of a 3-year-old. Which statement about pediatric airway anatomy is correct?
choices: The vocal cords are the narrowest point until age 12
The occiput is small, so padding under the head improves alignment
The trachea is longer and stiffer than an adult's
The tongue is proportionally larger and obstructs the airway more easily
quiz.why: A proportionally large tongue is a defining pediatric difference. The cricoid ring, not the cords, is narrowest until about age 8-10. The occiput is large, so padding goes under the shoulders, and the pediatric trachea is shorter and softer.

quiz.q: A 9-month-old with bronchiolitis has a heart rate that has fallen from 170 to 68 while you are preparing equipment. The most appropriate immediate action is:
choices: Apply the AED and analyze the rhythm
Begin bag-valve mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen
Recheck the pulse oximeter probe placement
Give a nebulized bronchodilator and reassess in 5 minutes
quiz.why: Bradycardia in an infant is almost always caused by hypoxia and it precedes arrest. Oxygenation and ventilation are the treatment. An AED is not indicated for a bradycardic child with a pulse, and rechecking the probe or nebulizing wastes the minutes that matter.

quiz.q: Why is aspirated material more likely to enter the right lung?
choices: The right lung has three lobes instead of two
The right lung sits lower in the chest
The right mainstem bronchus branches at a straighter angle
The left mainstem is normally blocked by the heart
quiz.why: The right mainstem leaves the carina at a straighter, more vertical angle, so gravity and momentum carry material into it. Lobe count and position of the heart do not determine where aspirated material lands.

quiz.q: A 55-year-old in respiratory distress can speak only two words between breaths, has crackles in both bases and pink frothy sputum. These lung sounds indicate:
choices: Fluid in the alveoli, most likely from heart failure
Bronchospasm from asthma
An upper airway obstruction above the cords
Mucus in the large airways from bronchitis
quiz.why: Crackles with frothy sputum are alveolar fluid, the picture of acute pulmonary edema. Bronchospasm produces wheezes, upper airway narrowing produces stridor, and large-airway mucus produces rhonchi that often clear with a cough.

quiz.q: Which respiratory rate is within normal limits for a resting 6-month-old infant?
choices: 10 breaths per minute
14 breaths per minute
18 breaths per minute
36 breaths per minute
quiz.why: Normal infant rates run 25-50 per minute. Rates of 10, 14 and 18 would be dangerously slow for an infant even though 14 and 18 are normal for an adult, whose range is 12-20.

quiz.q: A known asthmatic who was wheezing loudly now has a nearly silent chest, is diaphoretic and can barely stay awake. This means:
choices: The attack is resolving
Air movement has become so poor that no sound is produced; ventilate now
A pneumothorax has developed on the right
The patient is having a panic attack
quiz.why: Wheezing requires moving air, so the loss of wheeze with worsening mental status means near-total obstruction and impending arrest. It is never a sign of improvement. A pneumothorax would give unilateral findings, and a panic attack does not cause a falling level of consciousness.

quiz.q: A patient rescued from a garage with the car running is alert but confused, with an SpO2 of 100% on room air. Your interpretation is:
choices: The oximeter is reading carboxyhemoglobin as if it were oxygen; the patient is hypoxic
The patient is well oxygenated and the confusion is unrelated
The oximeter is malfunctioning and should be replaced
The patient is hyperventilating from anxiety
quiz.why: A standard pulse oximeter cannot distinguish carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin from oxygen, so CO poisoning reads normal or high while tissues are starved. Treat with high-flow oxygen. The device is working as designed; the reading is simply not meaningful here.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient ejected from a vehicle has gurgling respirations. Your first action is to:
choices: Insert an oropharyngeal airway
Perform a head-tilt chin-lift
Suction the airway with a rigid catheter
Begin bag-valve mask ventilation
quiz.why: Gurgling means fluid in the airway, and ventilating through it drives that fluid into the lungs. Suction first with a rigid tip. The adjunct and ventilation follow once the airway is clear, and this trauma patient should be opened with a jaw thrust, not a head-tilt.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time you should apply suction in a single attempt on a 4-year-old?
choices: 5 seconds
15 seconds
20 seconds
10 seconds
quiz.why: Children get a 10-second limit. Five seconds is the infant limit and 15 seconds is the adult limit. Exceeding these removes oxygen and can trigger vagal bradycardia.

quiz.q: During suctioning of an unresponsive adult, the heart rate drops from 88 to 44. You should:
choices: Stop suctioning and ventilate with high-flow oxygen
Continue suctioning until the airway is clear
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway and continue
Apply the AED
quiz.why: Vagal stimulation from the catheter plus loss of oxygen causes the bradycardia. Stopping and oxygenating reverses it. Continuing makes it worse, an NPA does not address the cause, and an AED is not indicated in a bradycardic patient with a pulse.

quiz.q: You insert an oropharyngeal airway in an unresponsive patient and she immediately gags and retches. You should:
choices: Hold it in place until she tolerates it
Remove it, roll her onto her side and suction as needed
Push it deeper past the gag reflex
Replace it with a larger oral airway
quiz.why: A gag reflex is an absolute contraindication to an OPA and signals a risk of vomiting and aspiration. Remove it, protect the airway by position, and consider a nasopharyngeal airway instead. Forcing it deeper or upsizing it worsens the problem.

quiz.q: The correct way to insert an oropharyngeal airway in a 2-year-old is:
choices: Upside down, then rotated 180 degrees
Sideways, then rotated 90 degrees
Right side up along the curve of the tongue, using a tongue blade
Through the nose with the bevel toward the septum
quiz.why: A child's soft palate tears easily, so rotation techniques are for adults only. Depress the tongue with a blade and follow the natural curve. The last choice describes an NPA, which is a different device.

quiz.q: A patient struck in the face has bruising around both eyes and clear fluid draining from the nose. Which intervention is contraindicated?
choices: Suction with a rigid catheter
Bag-valve mask ventilation
High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather
Nasopharyngeal airway insertion
quiz.why: Raccoon eyes and clear rhinorrhea suggest a basilar skull fracture, and an NPA can be pushed through the fracture into the cranial vault. Suction, oxygen and bag-valve mask ventilation all remain appropriate and are often urgently needed.

quiz.q: A nasopharyngeal airway should be measured from the:
choices: Corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw
Tip of the nostril to the earlobe
Center of the teeth to the earlobe
Bridge of the nose to the chin
quiz.why: Nostril to earlobe is the NPA landmark. Corner of the mouth to the earlobe and center of the teeth to the angle of the jaw are the OPA landmarks, and the last option is not a recognized measurement.

quiz.q: You place a nonrebreather at 12 L/min on a patient. The reservoir bag deflates completely with every inhalation. The correct action is:
choices: Increase the flow rate until the bag remains partly inflated
Switch to a simple face mask at 6 L/min
Remove the mask and use a nasal cannula
Do nothing; a deflating bag is expected
quiz.why: Total collapse means the patient's inspiratory demand exceeds the flow, so room air is being entrained around the seal and delivered oxygen falls. Raise the flow toward 15 L/min. Switching to a lower-concentration device gives a hypoxic patient less oxygen.

quiz.q: Approximately what oxygen concentration does a nasal cannula deliver at 4 L/min?
choices: About 21%
About 90%
About 60%
About 36%
quiz.why: A cannula adds roughly 4% per liter above room air's 21%, so 4 L/min gives about 35-37%. Twenty-one percent is room air with no supplement, 60% is the top of the simple mask range, and 90% requires a nonrebreather.

quiz.q: A simple face mask must be run at a minimum of 6 L/min because:
choices: Lower flows will not inflate the reservoir bag
Lower flows cause the one-way valves to stick
Lower flows let the patient rebreathe exhaled carbon dioxide from inside the mask
Lower flows dry out the nasal mucosa
quiz.why: A simple mask has no reservoir and no one-way valves, so flow must be high enough to flush exhaled CO2 out of the mask body between breaths. Reservoir bags and valves belong to the nonrebreather, and drying is a nasal cannula concern.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old with an SpO2 of 91% screams and pulls off every mask you place. The best option is:
choices: Blow-by oxygen at about 6 L/min held near the face, ideally by a parent
Restrain the child and hold the nonrebreather on
Withhold oxygen until arrival at the hospital
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway and attach oxygen tubing
quiz.why: A struggling, crying child consumes far more oxygen than the mask supplies, so blow-by delivered calmly is the better trade. Restraining worsens the distress, withholding leaves the child hypoxic, and an NPA is not an oxygen delivery device.

quiz.q: A D cylinder reads 1,200 psi. You are running oxygen at 10 L/min. About how many minutes remain before safe residual?
choices: About 19 minutes
About 16 minutes
About 28 minutes
About 34 minutes
quiz.why: 1200 minus 200 is 1000. 1000 times the D constant of 0.16 equals 160. 160 divided by 10 is 16 minutes. Forgetting to subtract the 200 psi residual yields about 19 minutes, and using the E constant yields about 28.

quiz.q: What is the safe residual pressure for a portable oxygen cylinder?
choices: Zero psi
50 psi
500 psi
200 psi
quiz.why: At 200 psi the gauge becomes unreliable and delivered flow falls off, so the cylinder is changed at or before that point. Running to zero risks losing oxygen mid-transport, and 500 psi wastes usable gas.

quiz.q: Which practice is unsafe when handling oxygen cylinders?
choices: Securing the cylinder in a bracket during transport
Opening the valve fully and then backing it off a quarter turn
Using petroleum jelly on a stiff regulator fitting
Storing cylinders out of direct sunlight
quiz.why: Hydrocarbons plus high-pressure oxygen can ignite without any spark, so no oil, grease or petroleum jelly goes near cylinders or regulators. The other three are all correct practice; a stiff fitting means a wrong yoke or a bad gasket, not a need for lubricant.

quiz.q: You are ventilating a 5-year-old who has a strong pulse but is not breathing. The correct ventilation rate is:
choices: 1 breath every 6 seconds
1 breath every 2-3 seconds
1 breath every 10 seconds
30 compressions to 2 breaths
quiz.why: A child or infant with a pulse is ventilated once every 2-3 seconds, 20-30 per minute. Every 6 seconds is the adult rate and under-ventilates a child. This patient has a pulse, so compressions are not indicated.

quiz.q: Which technique best prevents gastric distention during bag-valve mask ventilation?
choices: Squeezing slowly over about 1 second to visible chest rise only
Applying cricoid pressure throughout
Using a smaller mask
Ventilating at 20 breaths per minute in an adult
quiz.why: Gastric inflation is driven by excess volume and excess speed, so gentle one-second squeezes to chest rise are the fix. Cricoid pressure is no longer recommended, mask size affects the seal rather than the stomach, and 20 per minute hyperventilates an adult.

quiz.q: During CPR on an adult with a supraglottic airway in place, ventilations should be delivered:
choices: 30 compressions to 2 breaths with pauses
At 20 breaths per minute during pauses
Once every 6 seconds with continuous, uninterrupted compressions
Only after every third round of compressions
quiz.why: Once an advanced airway is in place, compressions become continuous and ventilations are asynchronous at 1 every 6 seconds. The 30:2 ratio with pauses applies only before an advanced airway, and 20 per minute would hyperventilate and reduce cardiac output.

quiz.q: An alert 71-year-old with a history of heart failure has crackles throughout, an SpO2 of 85% on a nonrebreather, a rate of 32, and a blood pressure of 178/96. The best next intervention is:
choices: Bag-valve mask ventilation at 10 per minute
Lay the patient flat and elevate the legs
Nasal cannula at 6 L/min
Apply CPAP starting at 5 cmH2O with the patient sitting upright
quiz.why: This is acute pulmonary edema in an awake, spontaneously breathing patient with a good blood pressure, which is the ideal CPAP candidate. Bagging an alert patient is unnecessary and poorly tolerated, lying flat worsens edema, and a cannula delivers less oxygen than the mask already failing.

quiz.q: Which finding is an absolute contraindication to CPAP?
choices: A systolic blood pressure of 82 mmHg
A respiratory rate of 28
An SpO2 of 89% on a nonrebreather
Audible crackles in both lung bases
quiz.why: Hypotension is a contraindication because the raised pressure inside the chest cuts venous return and can drop the pressure further. A fast rate, a low saturation and crackles are the findings that make CPAP indicated, not prohibited.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old at a restaurant is clutching his throat, cannot speak, and is making no sound. He is still standing. You should:
choices: Encourage him to cough forcefully
Deliver abdominal thrusts until the object clears or he goes unresponsive
Perform a blind finger sweep of the mouth
Lay him down and begin chest compressions
quiz.why: Inability to speak with no air movement is a severe obstruction requiring abdominal thrusts in a responsive adult. Coughing is the treatment for mild obstruction only, blind sweeps push objects deeper, and CPR is started only once the patient becomes unresponsive.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 62-year-old male, difficulty breathing
scenarios.intro: It is 0410. You are dispatched to a private residence for a 62-year-old man with difficulty breathing. Dispatch adds that the caller says he woke up unable to catch his breath and has been getting worse for about an hour. Your partner is driving. You have a full E cylinder, a nonrebreather, a bag-valve mask, a CPAP unit and a pulse oximeter in the bag.

steps.prompt:
You find him sitting bolt upright on the edge of the bed, leaning forward on his hands. He is pale and soaked with sweat. He can only say two or three words at a time. His wife says he takes a water pill and a blood pressure pill and had bypass surgery six years ago. His ankles are swollen and the veins in his neck stand out.

What is your first move?

choices.text: Leave him sitting upright and apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min while you listen to his lungs
choices.feedback: Correct. He is hypoxic and working hard but still moving air and fully alert, so the first step is high-concentration oxygen in the position he has already chosen. Never lay this patient down.

choices.text: Lay him flat on the stretcher and apply a nasal cannula at 4 L/min
choices.feedback: Two errors. Lying flat lets fluid redistribute through the lungs and worsens the hypoxia immediately, and a cannula at 4 L/min gives about 36% to a patient who is at 84%. Keep him upright and use a high-concentration device.

choices.text: Begin bag-valve mask ventilation at 10 breaths per minute
choices.feedback: Too aggressive for this moment. He is alert, breathing 32 times a minute on his own, and fighting a mask you force on him would be a struggle. Start with high-flow oxygen and reassess. Bagging is where this goes if he tires out.

choices.text: Ask the wife for a full medication list before touching the patient
choices.feedback: History matters, but not before an SpO2 of 84% and a patient speaking in two-word bursts. Treat the hypoxia while your partner gathers the history.

steps.prompt:
He is on the nonrebreather. You listen and hear wet crackles from the bases more than halfway up both sides, no wheezing. He coughs and brings up pink, frothy sputum. After three minutes on the mask his saturation has come up only to 88% and his rate is still 30.

What does this picture tell you, and what is the next intervention?

choices.text: Acute pulmonary edema from heart failure; set up CPAP at 5 cmH2O and coach him onto the mask
