choices.feedback: Right on both counts. Crackles, frothy pink sputum, distended neck veins, swollen ankles and a high blood pressure are the classic picture. CPAP pushes the fluid back out of the alveoli and unloads the ventricle. Start low and titrate.

choices.text: Asthma exacerbation; give a nebulized bronchodilator
choices.feedback: There is no wheeze and no asthma history. Crackles plus frothy sputum plus distended neck veins is fluid, not bronchospasm. A bronchodilator will not move alveolar fluid.

choices.text: Leave the nonrebreather on and transport without further intervention
choices.feedback: Acceptable only if CPAP is unavailable or he refuses it, and even then you are just watching him tire. He has been on maximum mask oxygen for three minutes with almost no improvement, which is the signal to add pressure.

choices.text: Suction the frothy sputum from his mouth with a rigid catheter and continue oxygen
choices.feedback: Suctioning froth out of the mouth is fine housekeeping, but the fluid is being generated in the alveoli faster than you can remove it. Suction does not treat the cause; pressure does.

steps.prompt:
You hold the CPAP mask against his face without straps and let him feel the flow while you explain it. He panics briefly, then settles when you keep talking to him. You strap it on at 5 cmH2O. Two minutes later he looks calmer, his rate is 26, and his saturation is 92%.

Your partner asks whether to change anything.

choices.text: Titrate the pressure up toward 10 cmH2O as tolerated, recheck the blood pressure, and continue coaching
choices.feedback: Correct. He is responding, so titrate within the 5-10 cmH2O EMT range and keep checking the blood pressure every 5 minutes, because CPAP reduces venous return. Coaching is what keeps the mask on his face.

choices.text: Remove CPAP now that the saturation has reached 92% and go back to the nonrebreather
choices.feedback: Taking the pressure away lets the alveoli collapse again and the edema returns, often worse. CPAP comes off when the patient deteriorates or arrives, not when the number first looks acceptable.

choices.text: Jump the pressure straight to 15 cmH2O to speed things up
choices.feedback: Above the EMT range in almost every protocol, and high pressure raises the risk of dropping his blood pressure and causing barotrauma. Titrate in steps and watch the patient.

choices.text: Hold the pressure at 5 cmH2O and reassess in 5 minutes
choices.feedback: Reasonable and safe. He is improving, so staying put is defensible. Titrating up as he tolerates it usually gets better results, but this will not hurt him.

steps.prompt: You are en route. Eight minutes into transport he becomes quiet. When you speak to him, he answers slowly and then closes his eyes. You recheck vitals and find his blood pressure has fallen substantially.

choices.text: Increase the CPAP pressure to overcome the worsening edema
choices.feedback: The opposite of what he needs. The high pressure in his chest is part of why his blood pressure fell, and a patient who cannot stay awake cannot protect his airway behind a strapped mask.

choices.text: Remove the CPAP mask and begin bag-valve mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen
choices.feedback: Correct. A falling systolic and a falling level of consciousness are both stop signs for CPAP. He now needs someone else to do the work of breathing for him, with an airway you can suction.

choices.text: Leave the mask on and recheck in 5 minutes
choices.feedback: Five minutes is a long time for a patient who is losing consciousness with a systolic of 86. By then you may be managing a vomiting patient in a strapped mask.

choices.text: Remove the mask, apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min, and monitor closely
choices.feedback: Removing the CPAP is right. But a sleepy patient breathing 20 shallow breaths with a saturation of 89% is not going to fix himself on a mask. He needs positive pressure ventilation.

steps.prompt: You have the mask off and are bagging him at one breath every six seconds. He vomits a small amount. Your suction unit is mounted on the wall and charged.

choices.text: Turn his head or roll him toward you, suction with the rigid tip for no more than 15 seconds, then resume ventilating
choices.feedback: Correct sequence. Clear it, keep the attempt under 15 seconds in an adult, and get back to ventilating. Watch for the heart rate to fall while you suction; if it does, stop early and bag.

choices.text: Continue bagging through the vomit to avoid interrupting ventilation
choices.feedback: This drives gastric contents into the lungs. Aspiration pneumonitis can be the thing that kills him three days from now. Suction first, always.

choices.text: Suction with the soft French catheter for 30 seconds to be thorough
choices.feedback: Wrong tip and wrong duration. A soft catheter clogs immediately on vomit, and 30 seconds of suction in an adult strips oxygen and can trigger vagal bradycardia.

choices.text: Sit him back up and let gravity drain it while you continue oxygen by mask
choices.feedback: Position helps, but he is no longer ventilating adequately on his own. You still owe him suction and positive pressure ventilation.

steps.prompt:
The airway is clear and you are ventilating him with an oral airway in place, chest rising with each squeeze. Saturation is climbing. You are four minutes from the emergency department.

What goes in your radio report?

choices.text: 62-year-old, acute pulmonary edema, initially on CPAP, deteriorated with hypotension and decreased consciousness, now bag-valve mask ventilated with an OPA, current vitals, ETA four minutes
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Age, working impression, what you did, how he responded, why you escalated, current status and ETA. The receiving team can set the room up before you arrive.

choices.text: 62-year-old with shortness of breath, will give details on arrival
choices.feedback: Too thin. This patient needs a bed with a ventilator and possibly nitroglycerin drips waiting. A vague report costs minutes on arrival.

choices.text: Read the full medication list and past surgical history over the radio
choices.feedback: Detail that belongs in the written report and the verbal handoff at the bedside. The radio report is the headline: who, what is wrong, what you did, how bad it is now, when you arrive.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: a patient in acute pulmonary edema is drowning in his own plasma, and the treatment ladder is position, then oxygen concentration, then pressure. Upright first, nonrebreather at 10-15 L/min second, CPAP at 5-10 cmH2O third.

The decision that separates a good EMT from a marginal one is knowing when to abandon CPAP. Falling blood pressure and falling mental status are not reasons to add pressure. They are reasons to take the mask off and bag. A patient who cannot stay awake cannot protect an airway behind a strapped mask, and the pressure that was helping his lungs is now starving his heart of venous return.

And through all of it: suction before you ventilate, count the ventilation rate out loud, and keep every suction attempt under 15 seconds in an adult.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: unresponsive male, possible overdose
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched to a report of an unresponsive male in the bathroom of a gas station. Police are on scene and report the area is secure. Dispatch states a bystander found him slumped against the wall and that there is drug paraphernalia visible. You bring the airway bag, oxygen, the bag-valve mask and naloxone.

steps.prompt:
He is a man in his twenties, slumped on the floor, lips and fingertips blue-gray. He does not respond to a shout or a firm trapezius pinch. His pupils are pinpoint. You watch his chest for ten seconds and count roughly six shallow, irregular breaths per minute. You feel a strong, slow carotid pulse.

What is your first intervention?

choices.text: Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min and prepare naloxone
choices.feedback: A mask does nothing for a patient who is not moving air. Six shallow breaths a minute is a ventilation failure, and after dead space almost nothing reaches his alveoli. He needs positive pressure now.

choices.text: Open the airway, then begin bag-valve mask ventilation with oxygen at 15 L/min
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the whole lesson of the call: his problem is ventilation, not oxygenation, so the bag is the treatment. Airway first, then ventilate. Naloxone comes after you have oxygenated him.

choices.text: Give naloxone immediately and watch for a response
choices.feedback: The reflex answer and the wrong order. Naloxone takes minutes to work, and his brain is hypoxic right now. Ventilate first. Many of these patients improve enough on the bag alone that the drug becomes less urgent.

choices.text: Begin chest compressions
choices.feedback: He has a strong carotid pulse. Compressions are not indicated. The bradycardia is a hypoxia response and it usually corrects once you ventilate him.

steps.prompt:
You tilt his head back and lift the chin. You immediately hear loud snoring, and when you look you see a pool of vomit and saliva in the back of his mouth.

What do you do before you put the mask on his face?

choices.text: Suction with the rigid Yankauer, no more than 15 seconds, applying suction on the way out
choices.feedback: Correct. You cannot ventilate through fluid and you must never bag it into his lungs. Rigid tip, under 15 seconds, suction on withdrawal, then ventilate. Roll him if there is more than you can clear.

choices.text: Place an oral airway; it will hold the vomit out of the way
choices.feedback: An adjunct does not clear fluid and it is not a barrier to aspiration. Pushing a plastic airway through a pool of vomit just moves it deeper. Suction first, adjunct second.

choices.text: Start bagging and let the positive pressure clear it
choices.feedback: This is how a bad airway becomes fatal. Positive pressure drives vomit into the trachea and the lungs. Suction first every time.

choices.text: Roll him onto his side to let it drain, then suction
choices.feedback: Reasonable, and a good move for high-volume vomit. Combined with rigid suction it works well. Just do not spend long on it, because he has been under-ventilating this entire time.

steps.prompt:
The airway is clear. The snoring stops when you hold the jaw forward but returns as soon as you let go. He has no gag reflex when you touch the back of his throat with the suction tip.

Which adjunct and which ventilation rate?

choices.text: Oropharyngeal airway sized from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, then ventilate once every 6 seconds
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. No gag reflex means an OPA is appropriate, and the correct landmark is corner of mouth to earlobe. An adult with a pulse gets one breath every 6 seconds, roughly ten per minute.

choices.text: Oropharyngeal airway, then ventilate once every 3 seconds to catch him up
choices.feedback: The adjunct is right, the rate is not. Twenty breaths per minute in an adult raises the pressure inside his chest, cuts off blood returning to the heart and drops his cardiac output. Every 6 seconds, counted out loud.

choices.text: Nasopharyngeal airway, then ventilate once every 6 seconds
choices.feedback: The rate is right and an NPA would not harm him, but with no gag reflex the OPA is the better airway; it holds the tongue more effectively and leaves the mouth accessible for suction.

choices.text: No adjunct; just hold the jaw and squeeze the bag
choices.feedback: You will lose the airway every time your grip tires, and you need that hand for the seal. This is exactly the patient an OPA was designed for.

steps.prompt:
Your partner takes over bagging with a two-handed C-E grip while you squeeze. After two minutes of good chest rise the saturation is climbing and the heart rate is coming up. He is still unresponsive and still not breathing on his own.

Your protocol carries naloxone as 4 mg intranasal or 2 mg intramuscular. What now?

choices.text: Administer naloxone per protocol while ventilation continues uninterrupted
choices.feedback: Correct. He is oxygenated now, which was the emergency. Naloxone reverses the respiratory depression, but it takes a few minutes and it never replaces ventilation. Somebody keeps bagging while the drug is given.

choices.text: Stop ventilating to give the naloxone, then reassess
choices.feedback: Never stop ventilating an apneic patient to free up a hand. One provider bags, the other gives the drug. He desaturates in under a minute without you.

choices.text: Skip naloxone; he is saturating at 94% on the bag
choices.feedback: The saturation is 94% only because you are doing his breathing for him. Naloxone can restore his own respiratory drive. Defensible if transport is two minutes away, but here it is the right drug.

choices.text: Give repeated doses back to back until he wakes fully
choices.feedback: Titrate to breathing, not to consciousness. Stacking doses precipitates severe withdrawal: vomiting, agitation and combativeness in a patient you now have to control in a moving vehicle.

steps.prompt: Three minutes after the naloxone he begins breathing on his own at 14 per minute with reasonable depth, then abruptly opens his eyes, rips at the mask and tries to stand. He is disoriented and angry, and he vomits onto the floor beside him.

choices.text: Stop ventilating, protect his airway by position and suction as needed, keep your distance and talk him down
choices.feedback: Correct. He is ventilating adequately now, so the bag comes off. Your priorities become airway protection from the vomiting, your own safety, and calm talk. Do not restrain him reflexively.

choices.text: Continue bag-valve mask ventilation despite his own adequate breathing
choices.feedback: Bagging a breathing, fighting patient forces air into his stomach and makes him vomit more. He is at 14 per minute with good depth. Stop and monitor.

choices.text: Give a second dose of naloxone
choices.feedback: He is already breathing. More naloxone only deepens withdrawal and makes him harder to manage, without any benefit to his respiratory drive.

choices.text: Restrain him immediately and load for transport
choices.feedback: Restraint is a last resort after de-escalation fails, and it carries real risk in someone who may vomit. Try talking first with police close by.

steps.prompt:
He calms down after a few minutes and now says he feels fine and wants to walk away. He is alert and oriented to person, place and time.

What is the critical teaching point you communicate to him and to the crew?

choices.text: Naloxone wears off in 30-90 minutes and often outlasted by the opioid, so he can stop breathing again; strongly encourage transport and document the refusal process carefully if he declines
choices.feedback: Correct and the reason these calls are dangerous. The drug that woke him has a shorter duration than what he took. Re-sedation is a real and documented cause of death after a field reversal.

choices.text: He is awake and oriented, so he is safe to be released with no further discussion
choices.feedback: This is the mistake that kills people. Alert now does not mean alert in forty minutes when the naloxone has cleared and the opioid has not.

choices.text: Tell him he must go to the hospital and that he has no choice in the matter
choices.feedback: An alert, oriented adult with capacity can refuse. Your job is to make the risk clear, involve medical control per protocol, and document thoroughly. Overriding capacity is neither legal nor effective.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to keep: in an opioid overdose the killer is hypoxia, not the drug. The order is airway, suction, adjunct, ventilate, then naloxone. Every one of those steps beats the syringe.

The specific numbers this call tested: six breaths a minute with shallow volume is a ventilation failure that no mask can fix; rigid suction for no more than 15 seconds in an adult with suction applied on the way out; an OPA sized corner of mouth to earlobe once you confirm there is no gag reflex; and one breath every 6 seconds for an adult with a pulse, no faster.

Two endings to remember. Titrate naloxone to breathing, not to consciousness, because a fully reversed patient is a vomiting, combative patient. And naloxone lasts 30-90 minutes while many opioids last far longer, so a patient who refuses transport after a field reversal can stop breathing again with nobody there.
